# In Sympathy

People think tuning a piano is about making notes perfect. It isn't. Perfect doesn't exist in a piano. A real string, when it speaks, is a little sharper than the math says it should be, so you stretch every octave — you tune the piano to what it is, not to what the theory wants. My father called it meeting the instrument halfway. He tuned pianos for forty years; I have done it for thirty-one; and the first thing I teach an apprentice is to stop listening for wrong and listen for the beat.

When two strings meant to be in unison are slightly apart, you don't hear two notes. You hear a wobble, a soft thrumming, like a moth against a window. That's the beat. It slows as the strings approach each other, and when it stops, that's it. That's tuned. Silence isn't the absence of sound. Silence is two sounds agreeing.

I took over my father's rounds when his hands went. Most of the pianos I inherited. One of them was the Drahos upright, a 1952 Baldwin in a house on Vinal Street, mustard siding, a dogwood over the porch. I was twenty-six the first time I opened its lid. I'm fifty-seven now, and I have been there twice a year for thirty-one years — sixty-two visits — and I never once sat at their table or learned what Mr. Drahos did for a living. I knew them through the piano.

The first decade, the piano told me a child was growing up. Fingernail scratches on middle C. A mug of pencils on the lid. Sheet music migrating from "The Happy Farmer" to a tattered Czerny to, one spring, the first page of the Moonlight Sonata, attempted with a courage the hands couldn't yet pay for. Mrs. Drahos would sit in the kitchen doorway with coffee and talk while I worked, and I learned the daughter's name was Vera, that she practiced before school, that the father considered the piano a luxury until the night of the sixth-grade recital, after which he turned the pages himself, badly.

Then Vera stopped. They always stop. Sixteen, seventeen — the piano went quiet. I came twice a year and the strings held their pitch like people holding their breath. Dust lay on the fallboard in a clean, untouched velvet. The metronome had wound down in the middle of a piece and no one had reset it, and it sat there for years at that half-finished tempo. Mrs. Drahos stopped talking while I worked. She'd say, "It hasn't been played," as if confessing.

The year Mr. Drahos died, she had me come in November, off schedule. The house smelled of lilies and of the medicinal sweetness of a body fighting something. The piano had gone sharp in the bass, the way a soundboard swells when the weather turns — grief has a pitch, it turns out, and it's about thirty cents sharp. She stood in the doorway and said, "He used to fall asleep to Vera playing. I want it ready. She's coming." I tuned that piano until every unison was a still, small pool. Vera came home and played, and I wasn't there, and I have always been a little sorry.

Then years. Yellowing. The Czerny gone, replaced by hymnals. Vera married somewhere out west; I knew this because a wedding invitation stood on the music desk for two visits running, then a photograph of a baby, then nothing. Mrs. Drahos's hands started to go the way my father's had. She'd ask me to press a few keys. "Does it still have it," she'd say, meaning the sound, meaning something else. I'd say it did.

The last time, the house was empty. Sold. She had gone to live near Vera, and the new people wanted the piano out, but her instruction, relayed by a nephew, was to tune it once more before it goes. I don't know why they agreed. Maybe the nephew was embarrassed to refuse a dead woman's — no. Not dead. Gone. A gone woman's wish.

I opened the lid in an empty living room. The wallpaper held a clean rectangle where the music desk had shaded it; the floor held the piano's outline in unfaded oak. The tall dust ghost. I set my fork against the wood and listened to A, and the whole piano was still there, still willing. One loose pin in the middle of the keyboard, one of the E's, wouldn't hold. I told it so. I tuned everything around it.

Here is the thing they don't tell you, or they do and you have to be fifty-seven and alone in an empty house to hear it. When you strike a note, every string on the piano that contains that note, in any octave, vibrates in sympathy. You can't see it — though you can lay a feather on the string and watch it tremble. Strike a C and every C the piano has ever had, high and low, shivers. Tuners call it sympathetic vibration. It is how the instrument agrees with itself.

I struck the A once more and laid my hand flat on the strings and felt the whole piano humming, the note I'd set and every ghost of that note besides, and I thought: sixty-two times. The recitals and the stopped lessons and the year it went sharp with grief, the baby's photograph, the wedding. None of it was gone. It was all still in there, in the wood and the felt and the copper winding of the bass strings, the way a struck note lives on in the strings it is related to.

I closed the lid. I wiped my fingerprints off the fallboard, which I had never once done, and left it for the movers. I did not look back. Looking back is for people who didn't listen.

My father, at the end, when his hands couldn't hold the lever, asked me to bring a piano to his room at the home. What they allowed was an electric keyboard. He had me tune it, which is a joke, because a keyboard doesn't go out of tune. I set it to A440 and told him it was perfect, and he said, "No, listen." And I listened, and there was no beat, and he closed his eyes.

"Meeting it halfway," he said.

She stood in the doorway and said, "He used to fall asleep to Vera playing. I want it ready. She's coming." I tuned that piano until every unison was a still, small pool. Vera came home and played, and I wasn't there, and I have always been a little sorry.

Then years. Yellowing. The Czerny gone, replaced by hymnals. Vera married somewhere out west; I knew this because a wedding invitation stood on the music desk for two visits running, then a photograph of a baby, then nothing. Mrs. Drahos's hands started to go the way my father's had. She'd ask me to press a few keys. "Does it still have it," she'd say, meaning the sound, meaning something else. I'd say it did.

People think tuning a piano is about making notes perfect. It isn't. Perfect doesn't exist in a piano. A real string, when it speaks, is a little sharper than the math says it should be, so you stretch every octave — you tune the piano to what it is, not to what the theory wants. It slows as the strings approach each other, and when it stops, that's it — that's tuned. Silence isn't the absence of sound. Silence is two sounds agreeing.

I took over my father's rounds when his hands went. Most of the pianos I inherited. One of them was the Drahos upright, a 1952 Baldwin Acrosonic in a house on Vinal Street, mustard siding, a dogwood leaning over the porch. I was twenty-six the first time I opened its lid. I'm fifty-seven now, and I have been there twice a year for thirty-one years, which is to say I have been to that house sixty-two times, and I never once sat at their table or learned what Mr. Drahos did for a living. I knew them through the piano.

The first decade, the piano told me a child was growing up. Fingernail scratches on C and D. A mug of pencils on the top. Sheet music migrating from "The Happy Stream" to a tattered Czerny to, one spring, the first page of the Moonlight Sonata, attempted with a courage the hands couldn't yet pay for. Mrs. Drahos would sit in the kitchen doorway with coffee and talk to me while I worked, and I learned that the daughter's name was Vera, that she practiced before school, that the father thought the piano was a luxury until the night of the sixth-grade recital and after that he turned the pages himself, badly.

Then Vera stopped. They always stop. Sixteen, seventeen — the piano went quiet. I came twice a year and the strings held their pitch like people holding their breath. Dust on the fallboard in a clean, untouched velvet. The metronome wound down in the middle of a piece and no one had reset it, and it sat there for years at that half-finished tempo. Mrs. Drahos stopped talking while I worked. She'd say, "It hasn't been played," as if confessing.

The year Mr. Drahos died, she had me come in November, off schedule. The house smelled of lilies and of the medicinal sweetness of a body fighting something. The piano hadn't been tuned in over a year and had gone sharp in the bass, which happens when the weather turns and the soundboard swells — grief has a pitch, it turns out, and it's about thirty cents sharp. She stood in the kitchen doorway and said, "He used to fall asleep to Vera playing. I want it ready. She's coming." And I tuned that piano until every unison was a still small pool, and Vera came home and played, and I wasn't there, and I have always been a little sorry.

Then years. The yellowing. The Czerny gone, replaced by hymnals. Vera married somewhere out west; I knew this because a wedding invitation was propped on the music desk for two visits running, then replaced by a photograph of a baby, then by nothing. I opened the lid in an empty living room. The wallpaper had a clean rectangle where the music desk's shadow had been; the floor had the piano's outline in un-faded oak. The tall dust ghost. I stripped the felt, set my fork against the wood, and listened to A, and the whole piano was still there, still willing. A loose pin in the middle of the keyboard, one of the E's, wouldn't hold. I told it so. I tuned everything around it.

Here is the thing they don't tell you, or maybe they do and you have to be fifty-seven and alone in an empty house to hear it. When you strike a note, every string on the piano that contains that note, in any octave, vibrates in sympathy. You can't see it. You can put a feather on the string and watch it tremble. The recitals and the stopped lessons and the year it went sharp with grief, the baby's photograph, the wedding. None of it was gone. It was all still in there, in the wood and the felt and the copper winding of the bass strings, the way a struck note lives on in the strings it is related to.

I closed the lid. I wiped my fingerprints off the fallboard, which I had never once done before, and I left the piano for the movers, and I did not look back, because looking back is for people who didn't listen.

My father, at the end, when his hands couldn't hold the lever anymore, asked me to bring a piano to his room at the home. An electric keyboard, was what they allowed. He had me tune it, which is a joke, because a keyboard doesn't go out of tune. I set it to A440 and told him it was perfect and he said, "No, listen."
